s01: Here is a question about one company, Kestrel Dynamics, and its internal documents.
What caused the billing delay in March 2026?
Let's ask a general AI model.
And it is completely made up.
s02: An AI model learns from public text, up to a cutoff date.
It has never seen your company's private documents.
So it does what it was trained to do.
It predicts the next word that sounds most likely.
Each candidate word gets a probability, and a likely one wins.
But sounding right is not the same as being right.
s03: The fix is surprisingly simple. Think of an exam.
A closed-book exam tests what you remember.
An open-book exam lets you look things up.
RAG turns every question into an open-book exam.
Before the AI answers, we find the right pages, and put them in front of it.
s04: R. A. G. stands for three steps.
Retrieval. Search your documents for the passages that matter.
Augmented. Add those passages to the prompt.
Generation. The AI writes the answer, using only what we gave it.
Let's follow our question through each step.
s05: But retrieval needs something to search, so we prepare ahead of time.
This project holds seven documents from Kestrel Dynamics.
A company overview, team charters, a security policy, and the March postmortem.
Each document is cut into smaller pieces, called chunks.
Why cut them? We want the exact paragraph that answers the question, not a whole file.
Every chunk is made searchable, and stored in one database.
s06: The system compares it against all eleven chunks.
Each chunk gets a score. How well does it match?
Sort by score, and keep the top six.
At the very top: the postmortem paragraph.
This project scores with three methods at once.
One matches words. One matches meaning. One follows connections.
Then it combines their votes. Each method gets its own chapter.
s07: We build a prompt. This is the actual text this project sends.
Answer only from the passages. Cite them. And if the answer isn't there, say I don't know.
Then the six passages, each with a number.
And the question, at the very end.
s08: The model reads about eight hundred tokens of context, and writes.
An expired TLS certificate on the Atlas API gateway caused authentication failures.
So the billing job retried until it ran out of retries.
See the small one at the end? That is a citation.
It points to passage one, so you can check the answer yourself.
s09: Put the two answers side by side.
With retrieval: the real cause, with proof.
Same model. The only difference is what we put in front of it.
s10: A fair question. Why not skip the search, and paste every document into the prompt?
Size. A model can only read so much at once, and a real company has thousands of documents, not seven.
Cost. You pay for every token the model reads, on every question.
Focus. Bury the right paragraph in a thousand pages, and the model is more likely to miss it.
And why not train the model on the documents instead?
Training is slow and expensive, and must be repeated whenever a document changes.
With RAG, a new document is searchable minutes after it arrives.
s11: So every RAG system has two phases.
Phase one, ingestion, happens ahead of time.
Documents in. Chunks out. Stored and searchable.
Phase two, the query, happens every time someone asks.
Search. Build the prompt. Generate the answer, with citations.
s12: And here it is, running in this project.
The same question, typed into the playground.
On the right, the passages it retrieved.
Each one shows its rank from every search method.
And the answer is marked grounded: one hundred percent.
s13: The model does not learn your documents.
Every time, we find the right pages, and hand them over.
That is RAG. An open-book exam for AI.
